blocks.prompt: How Something That Heavy Stays Up
blocks.text: An airplane is heavier than a house. It has no feathers. It does not flap. So how does it get into the sky? The answer is the wings. Each wing is tilted just a little. When the airplane races down the runway, the wings slice through the air and push a huge amount of it downward. The air pushes back. That push is called lift, and lift carries the airplane up. This only works when the airplane is going fast. That is why the runway is so long. The pilot needs room to get up to speed. Once the wheels leave the ground, the wings do the rest.

blocks.prompt: The Bicycle Shop That Built the First Airplane
blocks.text: In 1903, two brothers from Ohio built a flying machine in the back of their bicycle shop. Their names were Wilbur and Orville Wright. Plenty of people had tried to fly before them. Most of them thought the secret was a bigger engine. The Wright brothers thought the secret was steering. A machine that goes up but cannot be turned or leveled out is not a flying machine. It is a falling machine with a fan on it. So they practiced. They built gliders with no engine at all and flew them off the sand dunes at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, again and again, until they could hold the machine steady in the wind. On December 17, 1903, Orville lay flat on the lower wing and took off. That flight lasted twelve seconds and covered about 120 feet, which is shorter than the length of a big passenger jet today. Their fourth flight that day lasted fifty-nine seconds. The world changed on a cold beach in under a minute of flying.

4.title: How Something That Heavy Stays Up
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10

meta.templateLabel: How Something That Heavy Stays Up

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Four forces: lift, weight, thrust, drag
Roll, pitch, yaw: the three ways a plane turns
Ailerons roll it, the elevator pitches it, the rudder yaws it
Flaps let a wing lift more at slow speed
A loaded jumbo jet can weigh over 400 tons

blocks.prompt: Four Forces and Three Turns
blocks.text: Every airplane in the sky is arguing with four forces at once. Weight pulls it down. Lift holds it up. Thrust pushes it forward. Drag holds it back. When lift matches weight and thrust matches drag, the airplane cruises along steady and level. Change any one of them and the airplane climbs, dives, speeds up, or slows down. Lift is the strange one. A wing does not suck the airplane upward. It works by tilting slightly into the oncoming air and flinging a great mass of that air downward behind it. Air has weight, and pushing it down takes force, so the air pushes back on the wing with exactly the same force. That reaction is lift. Push enough air down, hard enough, and a machine weighing 400 tons rises off a runway. Steering is a separate problem, and it took the Wright brothers years to solve. An airplane can turn three ways at once. It can roll, tipping one wing down, using hinged panels near the wingtips called ailerons. It can pitch, lifting or dropping its nose, using the elevator on the tail. It can yaw, swinging its nose left or right, using the rudder. A pilot uses all three together. Turning an airplane is nothing like turning a car; you bank into the turn and pull the nose around with it.

it tilts into the air and flings a great mass of air downward, and the air pushes back
(inference: it has to shove enough air down each second, which needs speed)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Jets cruise near 35,000 feet, about six miles up
Cruise speed is around 560 miles per hour
The jet stream can blow over 100 mph, west to east

blocks.prompt: Six Miles Up, Where the Air Runs Out
blocks.text: A passenger jet spends almost its whole trip about six miles above the ground, roughly 35,000 feet. That sounds like showing off. It is actually the whole business plan. Up there the air is thin, and thin air pushes back less. Drag drops away, so the airplane can hold 560 miles an hour while burning far less fuel than the same speed would cost near the ground. Weather is mostly below you. And the strongest tailwinds on Earth live at that altitude: the jet stream, a river of wind that runs west to east at over 100 miles an hour. Riding it is why a flight from Los Angeles to New York is shorter than the same flight coming back. The price of thin air is that engines and people both need it. A jet engine solves this by grabbing enormous quantities of air and squeezing it. A fan the width of a small car pulls air in. Compressor blades pack it down to a fraction of its volume, which makes it fiercely hot. Fuel sprays in and burns. The exhaust blasts backward, and the engine is shoved forward. On a modern engine, most of the thrust does not even come from the burning part; it comes from the big fan bypassing air around the core, like an enormous propeller hidden in a tube. People are harder. At 35,000 feet the outside air is around 65 degrees below zero Fahrenheit and far too thin to breathe. So the cabin is a sealed tube, pumped up with air bled from the engines until it feels like sitting on a mountain about 7,000 feet high. Your ears pop on the way up because the pressure inside the tube is changing, not because the airplane is.

6.title: How Something That Heavy Stays Up
6.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: How Something That Heavy Stays Up

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Sir George Cayley named the four forces around 1799
Lilienthal made about 2,000 glides before dying in 1896
The Wrights' homemade wind tunnel tested about 200 wings
Three-axis control was the real invention, not the engine
The equal transit time explanation of lift is wrong
Wings are bend-tested far past anything a real flight does

blocks.prompt: The Wrights Did Not Invent the Engine
blocks.text: By 1900, flight was not a mystery of physics. It was a mystery of nerve. The four forces had been named a century earlier by George Cayley, an English baronet who worked out that a flying machine needed a fixed wing for lift, a separate source of thrust, and a tail to keep it pointed the right way. Engines had become light enough to matter. Otto Lilienthal had made roughly two thousand glides in Germany, hanging beneath a wing and swinging his legs to steer, before a gust stalled him in 1896 and killed him. The pieces were all on the table. Nobody could put them together. Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bicycle shop in Dayton, Ohio, and bicycles gave them the idea that everyone else had missed. A bicycle is unstable. It stays up only because the rider is constantly correcting it, leaning into turns, making a thousand tiny adjustments a minute without thinking. Every other experimenter was chasing stability: a machine so well balanced it would fly itself. The Wrights decided that was backward. Build a machine that the pilot flies, they reasoned, and then teach the pilot. That decision reorganized everything. It meant control came first and the engine came last. It meant hundreds of flights in gliders with no motor at all, off the dunes at Kitty Hawk, learning the feel of air the way you learn to ride. And it meant inventing three-axis control: warping the wingtips to roll, a forward elevator to pitch, and a movable rudder linked to the warping to hold the turn together. That system, not the engine, is the thing every airplane still uses today. The ailerons on a jet outside your window are doing Wilbur's job. They had one more advantage: they distrusted their sources. When their 1901 glider produced barely a third of the lift the published tables promised, they did not assume they had built it wrong. They built a wind tunnel out of a wooden box and a fan and tested around two hundred miniature wings themselves. The tables were wrong. Their own numbers were right, and the 1902 glider flew on those numbers. On December 17, 1903, at Kill Devil Hills, Orville flew about 120 feet in twelve seconds, less than the length of a modern jumbo jet's fuselage. Newspapers largely ignored it. The brothers kept flying anyway. It is worth noticing what a wing actually does, because the popular explanation is wrong. You have probably been told that air splitting over a curved top has farther to travel, must speed up to meet its partner underneath, and therefore drops in pressure. The parcels have no obligation to meet, and the math does not work. What a wing really does is simpler and more violent. It meets the oncoming air at a slight angle and throws an enormous quantity of it downward. Force in one direction, equal force in the other. Every second a jet is airborne, it is hurling tons of air at the planet, and the planet is holding it up in return. Tilt the wing too far and the flow tears loose from the surface, lift collapses, and the machine stalls. That is what killed Lilienthal, and it is exactly the failure the Wrights had trained themselves to fly out of.

(the reader has to trust the history first; correcting a schoolbook belief lands harder once the passage has earned credibility)
